nodes.title: Revisions
nodes.body: June 15 1996.  DMS | R. G. Gilmore; Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution

nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Scientific Name:  Citharichthys spilopterus
Common Name:  Bay Whiff

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum: Chordata
	Class: 	Osteichthyes
	Order: 	Pleuronectiformes
	Family:  Bothidae

nodes.title: Other Common Names
nodes.body:
Other:	Reference for Scientific Name (Gunther 1862).
	Reference for Classification (Robins et al.1991)

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial: None
Recreational:  None
Ecological Role:  Due to ubiquity and relative abundance this species may represent a significant component of the estuarine and marine food web (Tucker 1982).
Indicator:  None known

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  Atlantic, from New Jersey to Brazil, Gulf of Mexico, West Indies, and Caribbean sea (Martin and Drewry 1978).
Within Study Area:  Found throughout the Indian River Lagoon System (McNeese 1982; Christensen 1965; Mulligan 1981; Mulligan and Snelson 1983; Snelson 1983; Brown-Peterson and Eames 1990; Gilmore 1977; Gilmore 1988; Gunther and Hall 1963).
Mobility and Migration: Moves offshore in the winter and moves into shallow water during the summer (Martin and Drewry 1978; Hoese and Moore 1977).
Life Mode:  Common species of open sand/mud bottoms in estuaries and shallow continental shelf waters.

nodes.title: Habitat Type
nodes.body:
From inshore shallow water to 75 m usually over mud bottom.  In very shallow water found frequently near mangroves (Hoese and Moore 1977; Martin and Drewry1978; Robins et al. 1986).
Substrate:  Sand and muddy bottoms

nodes.title: Physical/Chemical
nodes.body:
Temperature: range from 4.1 - 35 C, with reports of 6 C causing mortality.
Salinity: Considered euryhaline with a preference for higher salinity but found in salinities 0.0 - 37 ppt, with the lower salinities at higher temperatures (Martin and Drewry 1978; Tucker 1982; Gunther and Hall 1963).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode:  Gonochoristic, oviparous, pelagic externally fertilized eggs.
Spawning Strategy:  Spawning can be inferred from the larval collection data of several researchers.  In the southern Gulf of Mexico spawning occurs in the fall, winter, and spring (Flores-Coto et al. 1991).  Off the Atlantic coast, spawning occurs from September through April in North Carolina and as late in May in Georgia (Tucker 1982; Reichert and Van Der Veer 1991).  Spawning most likely takes place in deeper offshore waters as the smaller larvae have been found offshore (Flores-Coto et al. 1991).
Fecundity:  No information.

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Egg: No information.
Larvae:  Larvae are pelagic.  During the early larval stage the right eye has not migrated.  In the later stage the larvae becomes a transforming larvae, where the right eye migrates to the left side of the head.  The right eye starts to migrate as early as 6.8 mm TL and reaches the final position from 9.0 -11.0 mm TL (Tucker 1982). Larvae have been found in temperatures of 4.1 - 26.6 C and salinity of 0.0 - 31.7 ppt in North Carolina (Tucker 1982).
Juvenile:  Juvenile stage begins after the right eye has migrated to the left side of the head, 9.0 - 11.0 mm TL (Tucker 1982).  The juvenile then settle in the shallow estuaries with a preference for settling on muddy bottoms with some plant material for cover.  In the estuaries juveniles may grow a mean of 0.72 mm per day at 24.5 C (Reichert and Van Der Veer 1991).
Adult: The adults reach a maximum of 200 mm TL (Martin and Drewry 1978; Hoese and Moore 1977; Robins et al. 1986)

nodes.title: Food Items
nodes.body: The primary food item is the mysid shrimp Neomysis americana.  This holds true except for the larger specimens over 125 mm TL where Neomysis is replaced by Trachypenaeus constrictus.  Other food items include other crustaceans and fish remains (Stickney et al. 1974).

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body: Due to ubiquity and relative abundance this species may represent a significant component of the estuarine and marine food web (Tucker 1982).
